html_source:
In brief

Parody. "Ga Ga Gara. Klook Klook Klook [...] Ga ga ga ga Gara. Klook Klook Klook": every parodic interruption in Cyclops so far has drawn on some elevated style or heroically exaggerated subject matter, but now the prose mocks Bloom's concern for animal welfare with onomatopoeic imitation of a clucking chicken and some simple childish sentences about a hen.

At more length

The interruption is prompted by the narrator's response to Bloom's opinions about how to treat the diseases of cattle and his air of humane concern for the animals' suffering. Of his veterinary opinions, the nameless one thinks scornfully that Bloom would "Teach your grandmother how to milk ducks." He turns Bloom's idea of touching animals gently when treating their sores into an image of thievery: "Gob, he'd have a soft hand under a hen." The onomatopoeia that follows brings the hen to life, and the childish sentences make her a friend to "good uncle Leo." It is not entirely clear whether the parody is mocking Bloom's soft touch or the narrator's contempt for his soft touch. Perhaps it is making light of the entire conversation about animals.

Gifford supposes that the passage may imitate "the style of a child's primer." This claim seems plausible enough and many other commentators have uncritically echoed it, but there does seem to be more to it. Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner note "various similar nursery rhymes" and quote one from the Oxford Dictionary of Nursery Rhymes:

Chook, chook, chook, chook, chook,
Good morning, Mrs. Hen.
How many chickens have you got?
Madam, I've got ten.
Four of them are yellow,
And four of them are brown,
The nicest in town.
Chook, chook, chook, chook, chook,
Cock-a-doodle doo.

As for the black hen laying an egg, still other genres may be involved. A. A. Milne's poem "The Little Black Hen" tells how "five big men" chase a hen to get her to lay an egg for them, but she eludes them and instead makes a deal with a child:

The Little Black Hen said,
What will you pay,
If I lay you an egg
For Easter Day?
"I'll give you a Please
And a How-do-you-do,
I'll show you the Bear
Who lives in the Zoo,
I'll show you the nettle-place
On my leg,
If you'll lay me a great big
Eastery egg."
The Little Black Hen
Said "I don't care
For a How-do-you-do
Or a Big-brown-bear,
But I'll lay you a beautiful
Eastery egg,
If you'll show me the nettle-place
On your leg."
I showed her the place
Where I had my sting,
She touched it gently
With one black wing.
"Nettles don't hurt
If you count to ten,
And now for the egg,"
Said the Little Black Hen.

Joyce would not have known this poem, which appeared in Now We Are Six (1927), but perhaps Milne knew other literary accounts of benignant hens laying eggs for appreciative children.

John Hunt 2026
